kangaroo-ca-2019-g0708-17.title: Use each rule
kangaroo-ca-2019-g0708-17.body:
- If Alex had no hat, Bob would wear one. Bob has no hat, so Alex **must** wear a hat.
- Bob has no hat, so by the second rule Carl wears a hat.

Both Alex and Carl wear hats.

**Answer: (A) Both Alex and Carl**

kangaroo-ca-2019-g0708-24.title: Exterior angles
kangaroo-ca-2019-g0708-24.body:
Walking around a convex polygon you turn through $360°$ in total. At a $120°$ angle you turn $60°$, at a $150°$ angle $30°$. With $k$ angles of each kind: $k(60° + 30°) = 360°$, so $k = 4$ and the polygon has 8 angles.

**Answer: (D) 8**

kangaroo-ca-2019-g0708-24.title: Angle sum
kangaroo-ca-2019-g0708-24.body:
An $n$-gon has angle sum $(n - 2) \cdot 180°$. With $n = 2k$: $k \cdot 120° + k \cdot 150° = (2k - 2) \cdot 180°$, so $270k = 360k - 360$, $k = 4$, $n = 8$.

**Answer: (D) 8**

kangaroo-ca-2019-g0708-25.title: Parity argument
kangaroo-ca-2019-g0708-25.body:
**18 questions suffice.** Ask for envelopes $\{1,2,3\}, \{1,2,4\}, \{1,2,5\}$ and then split envelopes 6 to 50 (45 envelopes) into 15 groups of three. Multiply all 18 answers: envelopes 1 and 2 appear three times each, all others once. Since $x^2 = 1$ for $x = \pm1$, the product of the answers equals $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_{50}$.

**Fewer do not.** The total product can only be found if some of the asked triples multiply to it, i.e. if we can choose some of the triples so that every envelope appears an **odd** number of times in them. (Otherwise one can change some of the numbers so that all answers stay the same but the total product changes.) If $T$ triples are chosen, the 50 odd counts add up to $3T$; a sum of 50 odd numbers is even, so $T$ is even. Also every envelope appears at least once, so $3T \ge 50$, $T \ge 17$. The smallest even such $T$ is 18.

**Answer: (B) 18**
